songs.title: Fire Away
songs.keyNote: Many online charts write this in G with capo 2 — they sound in A; on bass play the A notes below.
songs.feel: Slow soul ballad — big, sparse, let notes ring
songs.atAGlance: Intro (A E F#m D) → Verse 1 → Pre (Bm F#m E) → Chorus (F#m E A D E) → Verse 2 → Pre 2 → Chorus → Chorus → Outro, end on A.
songs.howToPlay: In 3/4, hit the root on beat 1 only and let it ring through 2-3. That's the record. As you get comfortable, add a soft 5th or octave on beat 3 in the choruses only. Verses: stay sparse. Do NOT play busy 1-2-3 patterns — the space is the groove. Good walk-ups: D → E → F#m into the chorus, and E → F# → A coming home.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the chorus first — it's the same 5-chord loop (6-5-1-4-5) the whole way. Once your hand knows F#m-E-A-D-E without looking, the verses are just 1-5-6-4.

songs.title: Neon Moon
songs.feel: Slow country ballad — lots of space, roots and 5ths, let notes ring
songs.sourceNote: Original version (Brand New Man, 1991). The 2019 Reboot version with Kacey Musgraves is in Eb — this sheet is the original, in A.
songs.atAGlance: Intro (A D A E) → Verse 1 → Chorus (D E) → Verse 2 → Chorus → Instrumental → Verse 3 → Chorus → Chorus → Outro, end on A.
songs.howToPlay: In 4/4, hit the root on beat 1 and let it ring — this is a slow ballad, and the space is the groove. Add the 5th on beat 3 once in a while (A→E, D→A, E→B) when the chorus lifts, and walk up D → E into the chorus. Verses: stay sparse. Do NOT play busy eighth-note runs — the record is mostly whole notes and long tones under the vocal.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the chorus first — it is the same D-E-A loop (4-5-1) every time. Once your hand knows D-E-A without looking, the verses are just 1-4-1-5-1. Only three chords in the whole song, so this one is a fast win.

songs.title: Say It Ain't So
songs.keyNote: Sounds Eb; guitar plays E shapes tuned down 1/2 step.
songs.feel: Quiet verses, loud choruses — follow the dynamics
songs.atAGlance: Intro (Cm G Ab Eb) → Verse 1 → Chorus → Verse 2 → Chorus → Bridge (Bb Bb/A Eb Gb) → Solo (loop) → Chorus → Outro, end on Eb.
songs.howToPlay: The verse is a laid-back, almost reggae skank — hit the root on beat 1 and let it ring, light eighth notes underneath. The chorus is a different beast: dig in, driving eighth-note roots, louder. The bridge builds and builds — walk up into it. The guitar is tuned down a half step and plays C#m-G#-A-E shapes; the concert chords below are what the bass plays in standard tuning.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the Cm-G-Ab-Eb loop first — it is the whole song except the bridge. Get the verse quiet and the chorus loud before you worry about anything else. The jump G to Ab (3rd to 4th fret, E string) is the one move to drill.

songs.title: The Middle
songs.feel: Driving pop-punk — eighth-note roots the whole way, don't let up
songs.atAGlance: Intro → Verse 1 → Chorus → Verse 2 → Chorus x2 → Solo (A D A D G D A) → Verse 3 → Chorus x2 → Outro, end on D.
songs.howToPlay: In 4/4 at ~162 bpm, play driving eighth-note roots all the way through — verses a little muted and tight, choruses open and loud. All three notes are open strings, so your fretting hand is free: the work is all in the right hand keeping the eighths even. Optional bass intro riff from the tab: A string 9-5-9-7-4-5-4-5, then straight into the verse.
songs.practiceTip: Loop D-A-G-D at tempo until the eighths are automatic — the whole song is that loop except the solo section. If 162 bpm is too fast at first, practice at 120 and work up; the pattern never changes, only the speed.

songs.title: Take Me Out
songs.tempoNote: Two tempos: verse ~122 bpm, riff ~104 bpm
songs.feel: Tense, staccato verse, then the famous chugging riff — the bass carries it
songs.atAGlance: Intro (Em, fast) → Verse 1 → Link → Riff/Chorus 1 → Verse 2 → Chorus 2 → Middle 8 → Hook x4 → Riff/Outro, end on Em.
songs.howToPlay: The verse is short, punchy notes — follow the vocal and stay tense. Then the tempo DROPS into the riff: steady chugging eighth notes on the root, Em-Am-Bm, and do not rush it. That tempo change is the whole trick of the song. F# shows up in the walk as D/F# — E string, 2nd fret.
songs.practiceTip: Practice the tempo drop on its own: count the verse fast, then settle into the riff at ~104 and stay there. Loop Em-Am-Bm until the riff is automatic — once your hand knows E-A-B without looking, the verses are just the Am-D-G-Bm-Em walk.

songs.title: Possum Kingdom
songs.timeSignature: 7/4 on the verse riff — count 7, not 4
songs.feel: Jagged and tense in the verse, straight-ahead quarter notes in the chorus. The riff is the song — lock in with the drums before you add anything fancy
songs.atAGlance: Intro riff → Verse 1 → Pre-chorus → Chorus → Verse 2 → Pre-chorus → Chorus → Bridge (Give it up to me, x3) → Instrumental → "Do you wanna die?" x8 → Final chorus → Outro, end on E7.
songs.howToPlay: The verse is one riff, over and over — E7, E7, E7, Asus4-A. Hit the root on beat 1 and ride it; the guitar riff does the moving, you hold the floor. Count the riff in 7 (1-2-3-4-5-6-7) or you will keep landing a beat early. The chorus is the release: steady quarter-note roots, F# - A - E - G#7, then A - D/F# - E7. The bridge walks up A - G#7 - C#7 - F#m - G#7 - C#7 - B, and the "Do you wanna die?" ending is just the verse riff again, louder.
songs.practiceTip: Count the verse riff out loud in 7 before you touch the bass — 1-2-3-4-5-6-7, E-E-E-A — until the 7 feels natural. Once the riff is in your hands, the chorus is just four quarter-note roots (F#-A-E-G#7) and the bridge is a straight walk up A-G#-C#-F#-G#-C#-B. The whole song is roots; the odd time is the hard part, not the notes.

songs.title: Truth
songs.feel: Gentle, quiet indie-folk — fingerpicked acoustic, low energy, lots of space
songs.sourceNote: Closing track (No. 10) on Luke Bower's debut album "Dopamine and Jesus" (Fair Trade Services, April 25, 2025); written by Luke Bower. Indie Christian folk / Americana — NOT a congregational worship standard, so no church chord chart exists. No published chart exists under the title "Truth"; chords follow the only published chart for this song's verses and chorus — the Ultimate Guitar chart for the album's companion track "Spirit," which uses the same opening verse and the same "spirit and the truth" chorus — transposed from its written key of B down into Truth's recorded key of Bb.
songs.atAGlance: Intro (Bb–Gm–F–Bb) → Verse 1 → Verse 2 → Chorus → Verse 3 → Verse 4 → Chorus → Instrumental → Verse 5 (outro, ends on Bb)
songs.howToPlay: Play the root on beat 1 and let it ring — that's most of the job. This song is quiet and reflective, so less is more: one root per chord change, long notes, no busy fills. Verses sit on the Gm and come home to Bb; the only lift is the Eb–F move in the middle of each verse, so a simple walk-up F → G → Bb into the next line feels great there. In the chorus, keep the same restraint — root on 1 for Eb, Bb, then F into Gm, and let the last line walk Gm – F – Bb back home. Match the singer's dynamics: verses soft, chorus just a touch fuller, final verse softest of all. Only four chords in the whole song — and three of the four roots sit at the 1st or 3rd fret. This is a stay-in-one-spot song.
songs.practiceTip: Learn the verse as one loop — Gm, Bb, Gm, F, Eb, F, Bb — and the chorus as Eb, Bb, F, Gm. Two little patterns cover all 3:42; after that, just listen for the singer's repeated tag lines at the end of each verse.

songs.title: To The Table
songs.tempoNote: SongSelect chart marks 67; automated analysis reads double-time 134 — play it at ~68
songs.feel: Slow country-gospel worship ballad — gentle, unhurried, acoustic-led, half-time pulse under a laid-back vocal
songs.sourceNote: Track 4 on "Chain Breaker" (2016). Written by Zach Williams, Jonathan Smith & Tony Wood. CCLI Song No. 7055780. Brian's name for it — "Bring It All to the Table" — is the chorus hook; the published title is "To The Table."
songs.atAGlance: Intro (A5–D2 x2) → Verse 1 (A–D, A–D, F#m–D, A–D) → Verse 2 (same, ends on E) → Chorus 1 (F#m–D–A–E x2, F#m–D–A, E/G#–F#m–D–A) → Verse 3 (verse loop, ends on E) → Chorus 2 (chorus loop) → Interlude (F#m–D2–A5 loop with A5/G# step-down, ends Esus) → Bridge x2 (F#m–D, A–E/G#, F#m–D, A–E/G#) → Final Chorus → Outro (A)
songs.howToPlay: Play roots only, and play them on beat 1 — this song breathes, so whole notes and half notes are your friends; never crowd the vocal. Verses: one soft root per chord change, nice and low. Choruses: root on 1 and 3 is plenty, a touch fuller as the band builds. Two passing notes do all the fancy work: on E/G# (the chorus turnaround and every bridge line) play G# — E string, 4th fret — and in the interlude the A5/G# is the same G#, a one-step walk-down A → G# → F# that leads you home. On Esus chords just play E (open E string) and let it hang — the suspense is the point. The record stays restrained throughout: the bass supports, it never shows off. End on a single A and let it ring out.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the chorus by itself first — F#m–D–A–E, roots on 1 and 3 — until the E/G# walk-down (G#, E string 4th fret) feels automatic. That one passing note is the only move in the song; once your hand knows it, the whole chart is yours.

songs.title: Chain Breaker
songs.tempoNote: Automated track analysis reads the beat double-time at 156 — 78 is the count to play
songs.feel: Slow-building Southern gospel-rock ballad — starts sparse with a pickup vocal line, grows through each chorus, peaks on the repeated bridge chant. Guitar charts often play G shapes with capo 5 — on bass there's no capo: play the concert C-major notes.
songs.sourceNote: Title track of "Chain Breaker" (2016). Written by Zach Williams, Jonathan Smith & Mia Fieldes.
songs.atAGlance: Verse (C–Am–G–F/G) → Chorus (C–F–C–G–C–Am–F–G) → Verse 2 → Chorus → Bridge chant x3 (C–Am–F) → Final chorus + tag (G/B and C/E slash chords) → Ending (C–F–C)
songs.howToPlay: Root on beat 1 and let it ring — this song lives in half notes and whole notes at 78 bpm. Verses stay sparse: root on 1, and as you settle in you can add the 5th on beat 3. Choruses open up — roots on 1 and 3, and walk C → B → A down into the Am on the "freedom" line. Treat every Gsus–G as a plain G root; the suspension is the guitar's job, not yours. The bridge chant is the build: steady quarter-note roots on the C–Am–F loop, a little stronger each time through, then drop back down for the final chorus. In the final chorus and tag, honor the slash chords — play B under G/B and E under C/E; those two passing notes are the lift at the end. Finish on C (A string, 3rd fret) and let it ring out.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the chorus first — C–F–C–G is the whole hook. Once your hand knows 1–4–1–5 without looking, the verses are just 1–6–5–4 and the bridge is 1–6–4 on repeat.

bassNotes.position: E string, 3rd fret (same root as G — the sus is the guitar's color)
Open E string (top / 4th string) (final chorus/tag only)

songs.title: East to West
songs.feel: Slow worship ballad — piano-led, quiet verses that build into a big chorus. Lots of space; let the roots ring under the vocal.
songs.sourceNote: Original version (The Altar and the Door, 2007) — written by Mark Hall & Bernie Herms. Note: this is Casting Crowns, not MercyMe — MercyMe has no song by this title. Casting Crowns re-recorded it with Ben Fuller in 2023, in Ab — this sheet is the 2007 original.
songs.atAGlance: Intro (F#m–Esus–E) → Verse 1 (D–E–F#m–A–D) → Chorus 1 (D–F#m–E–Bm) → Verse 2 (D–E–F#m–D) → Chorus 1 → Bridge (A–E/G#–F#m, D/F#–D–A, C#m) → Chorus 2 (E–A–E/G#–F#m–D) → Outro (F#m–E), end on F#m.
songs.howToPlay: This is a slow ballad, so the root on beat 1, held long, is the whole job — whole notes and half notes, let them ring and breathe with the piano. Verses stay quiet and sparse: one root per chord change, nothing busy underneath the vocal. The choruses open up — same roots, played with more weight, and you can add a soft root on beat 3 to keep the pulse. The one signature move is the walk in the verses: D → E → F#m rising into each line, so lean on that climb. In the bridge the bass walks A → E/G# (play G#, E string 4th fret) → F#m, then D/F# (play F#, E string 2nd fret) → D → A — follow those slash-chord bass notes, they're the movement under "I need Your peace." Final chorus changes key center to E–A — same roots, just don't autopilot back to the first chorus pattern. End on F# and let it ring out.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the verse climb first — D → E → F#m, root on 1, let each one ring — until the rise feels automatic. That three-note climb is under almost every line of the song; once your hand knows it, the choruses are just D–F#m–E and the whole song is in reach.

songs.title: No Half Steppin'
songs.tempoNote: Up-tempo — no published BPM (unverified); reviews call it bouncy and punchy
songs.feel: Driving soul-blues with horns and a hook guitar figure; shuffle-leaning groove, played with push
songs.sourceNote: Album version — opening track of the self-titled album "Sean Costello" (Artemis Records / Tone-Cool, released October 5, 2004; often catalogued as 2005). Written by Sean Costello (Night Latch Music). Running time 3:52. HONESTY NOTE: No published chord chart, tab, key, tempo, or transcription of this recording exists anywhere (checked Ultimate Guitar, Chordify, ChordU, PaidTabs, SongData, Shazam). Reviews describe an up-tempo, horn-driven soul-blues original — NOT a straight slow blues. The chords are the standard 12-bar blues framework written in A as a practice/jam version so you can learn the form and the feel. The recording's actual key, tempo, and exact form are unverified — confirm the key against the record before playing it with a band.
songs.atAGlance: (Practice form) 12-bar blues: A7 x4 → D7 x2 → A7 x2 → E7 → D7 → A7 → E7, repeat. Song shape: Verse 1 → Hook → Verse 2 → Bridge ("light" lines) → Hook → Verse 3 → Closing hook.
songs.howToPlay: Lock the root on beat 1 of every bar — that is non-negotiable, it is what holds a 12-bar together. The working pattern for this kind of up-tempo soul-blues is the classic shuffle walk inside each bar: root – 5th – flat-7 – 5th (in A: A – E – G – E), one note per beat, even and pushing, never rushing. Keep it simple under the verses, and let the pattern open up in the hook sections. Follow the standard blues dynamics: verses tight and in the pocket, hook bigger, and watch for stops — Vintage Guitar's review of this album notes a stop-time segment mid-song on this record, so keep your eyes up and be ready to hit beat 1 and lay out with the band. On the turnaround (last two bars), walk E7 down through D7 back to A7 and set up the next time through. If the record's key turns out not to be A, every pattern here moves with the Nashville numbers unchanged — that is the whole point of learning it this way.
songs.practiceTip: Loop one 12-bar alone with the A–E–G–E shuffle pattern until you can feel bar 9 (the E7 climb) coming without counting — then play along with the record and check the key with your open A string. If it clashes, move the whole pattern to the key your ear finds; the numbers never change.

bassNotes.position: E: open E string (the 5th); G: E string, 3rd fret (the flat-7)
A: open A string (the 5th); C: A string, 3rd fret (the flat-7)
B: A string, 2nd fret (the 5th); D: open D string (the flat-7)

body.heading: THE FORM (standard 12-bar blues — form guidance, not a transcription)

lines.note: Bars 1–4: A7 — stay home, pattern A–E–G–E each bar. Bars 5–6: D7 — lift, same pattern shape from D. Bars 7–8: A7 — back home. Bar 9: E7 — the climb. Bar 10: D7 — the fall. Bar 11: A7 — home. Bar 12: E7 — turnaround, leads back to bar 1 (or ends the song).
Common variation (quick change): D7 in bar 2 instead of A7. Either version is standard — listen for which one the band uses.

songs.title: Give Me One Reason
songs.keyNote: Sometimes spelled enharmonically as Gb major in charts; the sounding pitch is the same.
songs.feel: Laid-back shuffling blues-rock / soul-blues groove. The recording is spacious and unhurried: clean electric guitar carries the signature riff, the drums keep a steady shuffle, and the bass stays deep, simple and locked to the kick rather than busy.
songs.sourceNote: From New Beginning (1995), Tracy Chapman's fourth studio album, written by Tracy Chapman and released as a single from the album; it went on to win the Grammy Award for Best Rock Song.
songs.atAGlance: Instrumental intro, then three 12-bar blues verses, a guitar solo, four more 12-bar verses, and a short outro. The 'give me one reason' hook returns inside several verses, and the same 12-bar progression is used throughout.
songs.howToPlay: Play the root on beat 1 of every bar and sit on it, mostly roots with an occasional fifth or short approach note if you want it. Follow the 12-bar shape: four bars on F#, two on B, two back on F#, then the C# - B - F# - C# turnaround. Lock in with the kick drum, keep the notes even and leave plenty of space for the vocal and guitar riff.
songs.practiceTip: Count the 12-bar form in three groups of four bars, and learn the last four bars — C#7, B7, F#7, C#7 — as your turnaround cue. If you can hear and count that, you will never get lost, no matter which verse you are in.

songs.title: Born on the Bayou
songs.keyNote: Built on an E7 vamp with a Mixolydian, bluesy feel, so the chorus uses a natural D (bVII) rather than a D-sharp chord.
songs.feel: Laid-back but driving swamp rock in 4/4. The bass should sit deep and steady under the tremolo guitar riff, locking with Doug Clifford's drums and leaving plenty of space rather than overplaying.
songs.sourceNote: Written by John Fogerty. Opening track on Creedence Clearwater Revival's Bayou Country (1969); also released as the B-side of the 'Proud Mary' single.
songs.atAGlance: Long E7 intro, then Verse 1, chorus, Verse 2, chorus, a guitar solo over the E7 vamp, a final chorus beginning with the 'hound dog' lines, and an outro jam. Apart from the chorus tag of D-A-E7, the whole song sits on E7.
songs.howToPlay: Play a solid E on beat 1 and keep a simple, repeating root pulse on the open E string through the long E7 vamps - most of the song does not move. Lock in with the kick drum and stay out of the guitar's way. The only real movement is in the chorus, where you take the roots D (open D string) to A (open A string) and back home to E for each 'Born on the bayou' line.
songs.practiceTip: Loop just the chorus change D-A-E7 until the three open-string roots feel automatic, then practise counting through the long E7 vamps so you do not make the change early.

songs.title: Brown Eyed Girl
songs.feel: Bright, upbeat 1960s pop-rock in straight 4/4 with a light, bouncy lilt. The bass is prominent and buoyant, based mainly on roots with simple fifth/octave movement, and it gets a short featured break, so keep the tone round and the notes clean and dancing rather than heavy.
songs.sourceNote: Written by Van Morrison. Released as a single in 1967 and on his debut solo album Blowin' Your Mind! (1967).
songs.atAGlance: Intro (G-C-G-D), then Verse 1 and Verse 2, each ending with the C-D-G-Em / C-D-G-D 'my brown eyed girl' turnaround, then the 'sha la la' Chorus, a short bass solo/interlude, Verse 3 with the same turnaround, and a final chorus repeated to a fade.
songs.howToPlay: Play the root on beat 1 of every bar and keep it simple: the chords change one per bar, mostly G to C to G to D, so you can settle into that loop and lock in with the kick drum. At the end of each verse the chords step C to D up into G to Em, then C to D back to G to D — watch for that step-up. Add a fifth or an octave only once the root movement feels secure, and keep the pulse steady at this brisk tempo.
songs.practiceTip: Loop the four bars G-C-G-D slowly with a metronome, saying the Nashville numbers 1-4-1-5 as you play, then gradually work up to tempo; add the C-D-G-Em turnaround only once the main loop is automatic.
